cover.title: MYTHIC SPELLBOOK
cover.subtitle: Player's Handbook
cover.tagline: Everything you need to take your first turn — and your first thousand.

colophon: This handbook describes the live rules of Mythic Spellbook. Numbers in the Quick Reference are pulled from the game's own tables. Where the game and this book disagree, the game is right — and this book is out of date, so please tell us.

chapters.title: Into the Fray
chapters.blurb: What this game is, and what you will be doing in the next ten minutes.

sections.body:
Mythic Spellbook is a tactical card battler. You bring a deck of forty cards and a hero to a grid battlefield, summon units onto it, move them, and strike. Your hero holds the south edge. Your opponent's hero holds the north. Drop the enemy hero to 0 HP and you win. If yours falls first, the run ends there.

If you have played a collectible card game before, the cards will feel familiar. If you have played a tactics game — anything where units occupy squares and position matters — the board will feel familiar. Mythic Spellbook is both at once, and that is the whole idea: the card you hold is only half the decision. Where you put it is the other half.

A match is a back-and-forth of turns. On your turn you spend energy to play cards out of your hand, you move and act with the units you already have on the board, and then you end your turn. Your opponent answers. Repeat until one hero falls.

Most matches are decided by three things, in this order:

  1. Tempo. Did you spend your energy on something useful every single turn, or did you waste a turn holding a card you could not afford?
  2. Matchups. Fire scorches Nature. Water drowns Fire. Hitting the right element doubles your damage, and hitting the wrong one halves it. Over a whole match that is not a small edge — it is the match.
  3. The Kalon swing. You get three of them. Spent at the right moment, one transformation ends a game that looked lost.

sections.note: New player? Do these in order.
sections.body:
1. Play the tutorial battle. It walks the board, energy, movement and the Kalon in about five minutes. You can skip it, but do not.
  2. Take a starter deck. Do not build your own yet. A legal, coherent starter beats a clever pile of your favourite cards every time.
  3. Lose three matches on purpose. Push units forward, attack into bad matchups, burn your Kalons early. Learn what the board punishes.
  4. Then read Chapter IX and build something.

chapters.title: The Battlefield
chapters.blurb: The grid, the two heroes, the turn, and how a game actually ends.

sections.body:
The battlefield is a 14 × 12 grid. Your side is the south edge; the enemy holds the north. Your hero carries a gold outline, the enemy hero a red one. Everything else on the board is a unit — summoned by a card, belonging to one side or the other.

Distance is real. A unit with 2 movement cannot cross the board in a turn, and a unit with attack range 1 has to be standing next to the thing it wants to hit. Half of learning this game is learning how long it takes to get somewhere.

Reduce the enemy hero to 0 HP. That is the only win condition. Killing every enemy unit is a means, not an end — a board you have completely cleared still has not won you anything until you walk something up to the hero and finish the job.

The corollary matters more than new players expect: your hero is a target from turn one. A fast unit that slips past your line and starts chipping at your hero is not a nuisance to deal with later. It is the game.

Each of your turns runs in the same order:

  1. Turn start. Your maximum energy rises by 1 (to a ceiling of 10) and your energy refills to that maximum. Status effects that tick — poison, burn, bleed — deal their damage now.
  2. Your actions. In any order, as many times as you can pay for: play cards from your hand, and move and act with your units.
  3. End Turn. You hand the board to your opponent, who does all of the above.

There is no separate draw step you control and no combat phase you declare — you act, and the board resolves as you go. When you are out of things worth doing, end the turn. Holding energy does nothing; it does not carry over.

Sparkling ✨ event tiles appear on the field during a match. Walk your hero onto one to claim it — items, Cinder, sometimes a rare card. They are worth a detour, but notice what that sentence means: to collect one, your hero has to leave safety and walk into the open. That is the trade, and it is deliberate.

chapters.title: Energy & Your Hand
chapters.blurb: The resource that governs everything, and the five kinds of card you spend it on.

sections.body:
Every card costs energy — the number in its corner. You open the match on 1 energy. At the start of each of your turns your maximum rises by 1 and your pool refills to full, up to a ceiling of 10.

So the game has a shape built into it: lean early, explosive late. Turn one you can afford almost nothing. Turn eight you can drop a monster and still have change. A deck that ignores this — all expensive cards, no cheap ones — spends the first four turns doing nothing and loses before its good cards arrive.
sections.note: Energy does not carry over between turns. Unspent energy is wasted energy.

sections.body: You start with 5 cards drawn from your 40-card deck, and draw as the match goes on. Because your deck is forty cards and your opening hand is five, the card you built the deck around is probably not in your opening hand. Build so that a hand of cheap, ordinary cards is still a playable hand.
Everything you can hold is one of five things.

cards.name: Units
cards.text: Summon a fighter onto the board. It stays until it dies. Units are how you take and hold space, and how you eventually reach the enemy hero.

cards.name: Spells
cards.text: Resolve instantly and are gone. Damage, healing, buffs, debuffs, board removal. A spell is tempo in a can — no summoning sickness, no walk across the map.

cards.name: Traps
cards.text: Set face-down and lie hidden until their condition is met, then spring. Your opponent cannot see them, which means they also cannot play around them — until they get burned once and start playing carefully.

cards.name: Weather
cards.text: Rewrites conditions across the whole field, for both sides. Weather is not a private buff; if it helps your Ice units it helps theirs too.

cards.name: Locations
cards.text: Covers the board with terrain — a Lava Pit, a Sacred Grove, a Holy Spring. Like weather, a location is global. Only one is in play at a time, so playing yours removes theirs.

sections.body: Decks are finite. If a match runs long enough that your 40 cards run out, you begin taking fatigue damage instead of drawing. Very few matches get there — but if you are building a deck that intends to stall forever, know that the clock is real and it is pointed at you too.

chapters.title: Move, Then Strike
chapters.blurb: Unit stats, what a unit may do on a turn, and how damage is worked out.

sections.h: What a unit can do on your turn
sections.body:
Tap one of your units to open its actions. Each turn, a unit may move along a path and take one attack or ability. Not two attacks. Not an ability and then an attack. One.

Longer moves cost energy. Walking a unit clear across the field is not free — it competes with the card you wanted to play this turn. This is the tension the whole game runs on: the unit is in the wrong place, moving it costs the card, and playing the card leaves it in the wrong place.
Every unit and hero carries the same six numbers.

head: Stat
What it does
rows: Hit points. At 0 the unit dies and goes to the graveyard. On a hero, at 0 you lose.
Physical attack power. Checked against the defender's DEF.
Physical defence. Reduces incoming ATK-based damage.
Magic attack power. Checked against the defender's RES.
Magic resistance. Reduces incoming MAG-based damage.
Speed — governs movement distance, attack range and accuracy.

sections.note: A unit with high DEF and low RES is armoured against swords and naked against spells. Read both numbers before you commit an attacker.

sections.body:
Roughly, in this order:

  1. The attacker's ATK (or MAG) is checked against the defender's DEF (or RES).
  2. The elemental matchup is applied — ×2 if you are strong against them, ×0.5 if they resist you, ×1 otherwise. See Chapter V.
  3. Status effects, passives, held items, weather and the active location adjust the result.
  4. Accuracy is rolled. Attacks can miss, and several statuses make misses much more likely.

The practical lesson is step 2. A weak unit swinging into a favourable matchup routinely out-damages a strong unit swinging into an unfavourable one. Check the element before you check the stat line.

Three habits separate players who win close games from players who lose them:

  • Do not walk into range for nothing. If you move up and cannot attack this turn, you have handed your opponent a free swing.
  • Screen your hero. Keep a body between the enemy's fastest unit and your hero. Always.
  • Count their movement, not yours. The question is never "can I reach them" — it is "what can reach me after I do this."

chapters.title: The Twenty-One Elements
chapters.blurb: The matchup wheel. The single most important table in this book.

sections.body:
Every unit, hero and most spells carry one or more elements. When an attack lands, the attacker's element is compared to the defender's:

  • ×2.0 — super-effective. The attacker is strong against that element.
  • ×0.5 — resisted. The defender is strong against the attacker.
  • ×1.0 — neutral. Everything else.

A handful of pairs are sworn opposites — each is super-effective against the other, so both directions hit for ×2 and neither resists. Light and Shadow are the classic pair. Those fights are decided entirely by who swings first.
sections.note: Doubling your damage is the largest single swing available to you in this game, and it is free. It costs nothing but attacking the right target.

sections.body: Every element, what it beats, and what beats it. Generated from the live game tables.

Elements are not only about damage — several are flatly immune to statuses that would otherwise cripple them. Fire cannot be Burned. Nature cannot be Poisoned. Metal has no flesh to Bleed and no blood to poison. Storm cannot be Stunned. Ice is already cold, so Slow and Freeze do nothing to it.

This is why a status-heavy deck can fall apart against the wrong board: your entire plan reads as blank text on a unit that shrugs it off.

chapters.title: Factions
chapters.blurb: The forty-two tribes, and why your deck should care about them.

sections.body:
Where an element decides how hard you hit, a faction decides who you hit alongside. Factions are the tribal axis: cards, passives and held items reward you for stacking them. A Dragonblood charm is a decent buff on anything and a large one on a Dragonkin. A commander that rallies Undead does nothing in a deck with one skeleton in it.

A unit can carry more than one faction — a Goblin King is both Goblinoid and Warrior, and counts for both.

chapters.title: Status Effects
chapters.blurb: Everything that can be stuck on a unit, good and bad.

sections.body:
Statuses sit on a unit as icons and last a set number of turns unless something clears them. They come in four rough shapes:

  • Damage over time — Poison, Burn, Bleed, Siphoned. They tick at turn start. Three turns of Burn is nine damage the enemy never had to roll for.
  • Control — Stun, Freeze, Sleep, Confusion, Paralysis. They take turns away. A stunned unit is, for that turn, a card you never played.
  • Stat swings — Weak, Strong, Shielded, Focused, Infected. They move the numbers that damage is calculated from.
  • Stances and hexes — Protected, Countering, Ambush Guard, Rage, Corrupted, Spectral Haze. These change the rules for that unit, not just its numbers.
sections.note: Control is the strongest category and the reason immunities exist. Before you build around Freeze, check how many Ice and Crystal units the field is full of.

chapters.title: The Kalon Swing
chapters.blurb: Three transformations a match. This is the game's signature move.
chapters.art: assets/artwork/Abraxas Creator of Source Kalon Mode.png

sections.body:
You hold three Kalon uses per match. Spend one to transform an eligible unit into its secret form — bigger stats, new moves, sometimes an entirely different faction. A Goblin Scout becomes the Goblin King. A Dire Wolf becomes the Alpha. The unit keeps its position and its place in your line; everything else about it changes.

The Kalon Source is this game's turn-stealer, and the reason a board that looks lost is not necessarily lost.

• Three per match, not three per turn — and at most one per turn.
  • Only eligible units can transform. Not every card has a Kalon form; the ones that do show it.
  • Certain cards and effects can seal your Kalons for a number of your turns. While sealed, no transformation happens at any price.
  • A few effects grant Kalon charges back, and a few units are forced to ascend by an outside trigger. Your ceiling is still three held at once.

sections.note: The most common new-player mistake in the game is burning a Kalon on turn two because it was available.
sections.body:
A Kalon is not a play you make because you can. It is a play you make because it changes the outcome. Good moments:

  • To break a stalemate. Two lines are staring at each other and neither can profitably attack. A transformation makes an attack profitable.
  • To survive lethal. The transformed form has more HP. A unit about to die becomes one that lives and swings back.
  • To flip a matchup. Some forms change element or faction outright — an attack that was resisted becomes super-effective.

Bad moments: to make a good trade slightly better; to win a fight you were already winning; because the button was glowing.

chapters.title: Building a Deck
chapters.blurb: Forty cards, three copies, and the discipline to cut your favourites.

sections.body:
Two rules, no exceptions:

  • A deck is exactly 40 cards. Not 39, not 41. A deck that is not exactly 40 cannot be taken into a match.
  • At most 3 copies of any one card.
Because energy climbs by one per turn, your deck needs something to do on every turn, not just the good ones. A workable shape for a 40-card deck:

head: Cost
Roughly how many
Why
rows: Your first three turns. Without these you simply pass.
The body of the deck. Most of your real cards live here.
Finishers. More than a handful and you brick.

sections.note: If you are unsure, cut an expensive card and add a cheap one. Decks lose far more often to a dead turn three than to a missing bomb on turn nine.

sections.body:
The temptation is to play one element so that every buff and synergy lines up. The danger is that one element means one weakness — and the five things that beat it beat your entire deck.

A reasonable default: one primary element for your core and synergies, plus a secondary chosen specifically to cover your primary's worst matchups. Look up your primary in Chapter V, read its Weak to row, and pick a secondary that is strong against those.

• Early bodies. Something to put on the board on turns 1–3 so you are not conceding the field.
  • Reach. At least a few ways to damage something you are not standing next to — spells, or units with range.
  • An answer to a big unit. Every format has one. If your deck cannot remove or out-trade it, you lose to it every time.
  • Kalon targets. Cards with Kalon forms, in numbers. Three charges you can never use are three charges you do not have.

The hard part of deckbuilding is not choosing 40 cards. It is choosing the 40th. When you are one over, cut:

  1. The card you have never actually been happy to draw.
  2. The second copy of something situational.
  3. The most expensive card in the deck, before anything cheap.
  4. The card that only works if another specific card is also in play.

chapters.title: Cards, Rarity & Packs
chapters.blurb: Where cards come from and what the colours on them mean.

sections.h: What rarity does and does not mean
sections.body:
Rarity tells you how hard a card is to get. It does not promise the card is good in your deck. A Common that costs 1 and holds a lane is worth more to a working deck than a Mythic you cannot afford until turn nine.

What rarity does reliably track is scale: higher rarities tend to carry bigger stat lines, more elaborate abilities and more generous loot when defeated.

• Packs — bought and opened from the shop. The headline way to get new cards.
  • Battle rewards — matches, campaign nodes and daily challenges pay out cards as well as Cinder.
  • The Incubator — cores hatch into cards after a number of battles.
  • The Player Market and Card Shops — buy directly from other players for Cinder. Unlocks as you level heroes.

chapters.title: Heroes, Items & Fatigue
chapters.blurb: Your hero is a persistent character, not a health bar.

sections.body: Your heroes persist between matches. They gain levels, learn moves at set levels and carry their progress with them. Hero level also gates parts of the game: the Camp opens at hero or account Lv 3, the Tutor Shop at account Lv 5, the Cashout Vault at hero Lv 15, and the Player Market at two heroes at Lv 15.
A hero can carry a held item into battle. Items are small, permanent-feeling edges rather than game-winners — and the defensive ones are often the better pick.

head: Item
Effect
rows: Heals 15 HP once per battle when below 30% HP
Survive one lethal blow at 1 HP, once per battle

sections.note: Focus Sash and Healing Berry win more matches than the flat +5s. A stat bonus improves a fight you were already having; a survival trigger gives you a turn you were not going to get.

sections.body:
Every battle tires a hero. This is the system that stops you running one favourite hero forever.

  • Past a fatigue threshold a hero deploys 🩹 Injured and takes double damage from everything for that match.
  • Fatigue falls on its own — a fully spent hero is clear in 24 hours, and half-spent in half that.
  • Exhausted heroes (out of battle slots) take −2 to every primary stat.
  • Stressed heroes pay +1 energy per card in battle at 50+ stress, and +2 at 80+.

The design intent is plain: rotate your roster. Three rested heroes beat one exhausted one, every time.

chapters.title: The World Outside Battle
chapters.blurb: Seven portals, and what each one is actually for.

sections.body: The main menu opens onto seven places. You do not need all of them on day one — Battle Hall and Forge Sanctum will carry you a long way.

cards.name: Battle Hall
cards.text: Fight, climb, win the day. Quick Battle, the campaign, Play Online, the Colosseum, Gym Core Wars, Ethos Heights and the Season Pass all live here.

cards.name: Forge Sanctum
cards.text: Craft cards, moves, sprites and decks. This is where you build and edit your 40-card lists — and where the Incubator hatches cores.

cards.name: Card Shop
cards.text: Run your own storefront and visit shops other players own, buying their cards for Cinder. Open to everyone from the start.

cards.name: Ruin Exchange
cards.text: Trade, sell and cash out. The Player Market and the Cashout Vault sit behind hero-level gates.

cards.name: The Codex
cards.text: Inventory, bestiary and trophies. Your record of everything you have collected and everything you have beaten.

cards.name: The Camp
cards.text: Roster, replays and leaders. Manage your heroes, rest them, and rewatch your matches. Opens at Lv 3.

cards.name: Arcanum
cards.text: Settings and data. Account, options, saves.

sections.body:
• Quick Battle — pick a deck, jump in. The fastest loop in the game.
  • The Campaign — chapters of nodes with fixed opponents. The best place to learn matchups without a ladder rating on the line.
  • Play Online — real opponents, live.
  • The Colosseum — ranked competition and divisions.
  • Gym Core Wars — core-based challenge fights.
  • Ethos Heights — a roguelite run through the city, taking districts back from the factions.
  • Daily Challenge — one a day, with a modifier attached. "Energy Surge" gives both sides +2 max energy per turn instead of +1, which turns the whole curve on its head.

chapters.title: Cinder
chapters.blurb: The currency, where it comes from, and what it is worth.

sections.body: Cinder is the game's currency. You earn it by playing — battles, campaign nodes, daily challenges, event tiles, selling cards to other players — and you spend it on packs, shop stock, market purchases and services.

• Packs — the main sink, and the main way a new collection grows.
  • The Player Market and Card Shops — buying a specific card you need beats opening packs and hoping.
  • Services and upgrades — the Tutor Shop and the rest of the Ruin Exchange.
sections.note: If you are short on Cinder and short on cards, buy the specific card your deck is missing rather than a pack. A deck with its last slot filled wins more games than a deck with one more random Rare in the pile.

chapters.title: Quick Reference
chapters.blurb: The whole game on one page. Print this.

sections.body:
1. Spend all your energy every turn, or have a real reason not to.
  2. Check the element before you check the stat line.
  3. Never leave your hero unscreened.
  4. Moving costs energy. Count it before you commit.
  5. A unit moves and acts once — never twice.
  6. Do not walk into range if you cannot attack this turn.
  7. Save your Kalons for a moment that changes the result.
  8. Cut the expensive card, not the cheap one.
  9. Cover your primary element's weaknesses with your secondary.
  10. Rotate your heroes. Fatigue is real and it doubles the damage you take.
